prompt: Which factor of production consists of natural resources used in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Capital

options.label: B
options.text: Enterprise

options.label: C
options.text: Labour

options.label: D
options.text: Land

explanation: Land is the factor of production made up of natural resources. It includes resources such as agricultural land, forests, rivers, mineral deposits and other gifts of nature used to produce goods and services.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which factor of production is the human resource used in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Enterprise

options.label: B
options.text: Land

options.label: C
options.text: Capital

options.label: D
options.text: Labour

explanation: Labour is the human resource used in production. It refers to the physical and mental effort supplied by people when producing goods and services.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which item is an example of physical capital?

options.label: A
options.text: A factory’s cutting machine.

options.label: B
options.text: A worker’s engineering qualification.

options.label: C
options.text: A manager’s acquired experience.

options.label: D
options.text: An employee’s literacy skills.

explanation: Physical capital consists of man-made assets used to assist production, such as machinery, tools and factory buildings. Qualifications, experience and skills form part of human capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is the reward to labour?

options.label: A
options.text: Interest payments.

options.label: B
options.text: Wage payments.

options.label: C
options.text: Profit receipts.

options.label: D
options.text: Rental receipts.

explanation: Labour receives wages or salaries as its factor reward. Rent is associated with land, interest with capital and profit with enterprise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is division of labour?

options.label: A
options.text: Replacing workers with automated production equipment.

options.label: B
options.text: Assigning every worker the complete production process.

options.label: C
options.text: Splitting production into separate specialist tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: Producing every good needed without exchange.

explanation: Division of labour occurs when a production process is broken into separate tasks and workers specialise in particular tasks rather than each worker completing the whole product.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which is a main role of an entrepreneur?

options.label: A
options.text: Supplying natural resources without organising their use.

options.label: B
options.text: Performing routine tasks for an agreed wage.

options.label: C
options.text: Receiving a guaranteed return without business risk.

options.label: D
options.text: Organising land, labour and capital for production.

explanation: An entrepreneur organises land, labour and capital so that production can take place. The entrepreneur also bears or accepts business risk.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which factor of production includes a firm's delivery vans used to distribute its products?

options.label: A
options.text: Capital

options.label: B
options.text: Labour

options.label: C
options.text: Enterprise

options.label: D
options.text: Land

explanation: Capital is any man-made aid to production. Delivery vans used by a firm to help produce and distribute its output are therefore capital goods.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which change most directly increases human capital?

options.label: A
options.text: Providing additional vocational training to workers.

options.label: B
options.text: Renting additional factory premises for production.

options.label: C
options.text: Buying additional vehicles to distribute products.

options.label: D
options.text: Discovering additional mineral resources for extraction.

explanation: Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge and abilities embodied in people. Vocational training directly increases those skills, whereas vehicles and buildings are physical capital and a mineral deposit is land.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is the reward to land?

options.label: A
options.text: Rent

options.label: B
options.text: Wages

options.label: C
options.text: Interest

options.label: D
options.text: Profit

explanation: The conventional factor reward to land is rent. The other rewards are wages to labour, interest to capital and profit to enterprise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which is most likely to be an advantage of specialisation by a worker?

options.label: A
options.text: Less dependence on exchange with other producers.

options.label: B
options.text: Greater proficiency and productivity in the chosen task.

options.label: C
options.text: Less need to adapt to new production technology.

options.label: D
options.text: Greater ability to produce every required good independently.

explanation: Specialisation allows individuals to concentrate on tasks in which they have an advantage. This can raise output and productivity, but it also increases dependence on exchange and does not remove the risk that specialist skills become obsolete.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A forest used to supply timber to a furniture producer is classified as which factor of production?

options.label: A
options.text: Enterprise

options.label: B
options.text: Land

options.label: C
options.text: Labour

options.label: D
options.text: Physical capital

explanation: Land includes natural resources such as forests. Even though timber is later processed by firms, the forest itself is a natural resource and therefore land.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which pair consists only of human capital?

options.label: A
options.text: A nurse's training and a programmer's coding skills

options.label: B
options.text: The training completed by a qualified nurse and the scanning machinery installed in the hospital where that nurse works

options.label: C
options.text: A computer server and a programmer's coding skills

options.label: D
options.text: A factory building and a manager's experience

explanation: Human capital refers to the knowledge, skills and abilities embodied in people. Training and coding skills are both human capital; scanners, servers and buildings are physical capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is the reward to capital?

options.label: A
options.text: Wages

options.label: B
options.text: Profit

options.label: C
options.text: Interest

options.label: D
options.text: Rent

explanation: Interest is the conventional reward to capital. Rent is the reward to land, wages to labour and profit to enterprise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which situation is an example of specialisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Producing everything consumed without exchanging any goods.

options.label: B
options.text: Producing bread and obtaining other goods through exchange.

options.label: C
options.text: Providing every household need through its own production.

options.label: D
options.text: Requiring every employee to perform every production task.

explanation: Specialisation occurs when an individual, firm, region or country concentrates on producing some goods or services rather than others. The baker then relies on exchange to obtain other products.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why does an entrepreneur face risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Resources are committed after sales revenue becomes certain.

options.label: B
options.text: Resources are supplied without any alternative productive uses.

options.label: C
options.text: Resources are committed before sales revenue becomes certain.

options.label: D
options.text: Resources are hired without any wages or rental costs.

explanation: Production decisions are made before all outcomes are known. The entrepreneur commits resources without a guarantee that future sales revenue will cover costs, so profit is uncertain.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which item is labour rather than capital?

options.label: A
options.text: A workshop used for construction projects.

options.label: B
options.text: A ladder used on construction sites.

options.label: C
options.text: An electric drill used in installation.

options.label: D
options.text: An electrician’s work on installation tasks.

explanation: The electrician's work is human effort and therefore labour. The drill, workshop and ladder are man-made aids to production and are physical capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which change increases physical capital but not human capital?

options.label: A
options.text: Employees complete a technical apprenticeship that increases their skills while the stock of production machinery remains unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Workers attend an advanced skills course.

options.label: C
options.text: A manufacturer installs additional production machinery.

options.label: D
options.text: Technicians gain experience using existing equipment.

explanation: A robot is a man-made aid to production and therefore physical capital. Training, experience and apprenticeships improve the skills embodied in workers and therefore increase human capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is the reward to enterprise?

options.label: A
options.text: Rent

options.label: B
options.text: Interest

options.label: C
options.text: Wages

options.label: D
options.text: Profit

explanation: Profit is the reward to enterprise for organising production and bearing risk. The other factor rewards are rent to land, interest to capital and wages to labour.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which is most likely to be a disadvantage of division of labour for workers?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher output from greater task proficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Greater boredom from repetitive specialist tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater independence from other production stages.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower risk of skills becoming technologically obsolete.

explanation: When production is divided into narrow repetitive tasks, workers may become bored or dissatisfied. The coursebook also notes that workers may become deskilled even though division of labour can raise output.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: In a large company, salaried managers organise production while shareholders bear much of the financial risk. What does this illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ownership converts the shareholders’ investment into natural resources.

options.label: B
options.text: Large-scale production removes the need for entrepreneurial organisation.

options.label: C
options.text: Salaried managers automatically receive the firm’s entire residual profit because organising production eliminates shareholders’ exposure to losses.

options.label: D
options.text: Organisation and risk-bearing can be performed by different people.

explanation: In small firms one entrepreneur may both organise the factors and bear risk. In larger firms these functions can be separated, with managers organising production and owners or shareholders bearing the financial risk.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Oil beneath the ground is classified as which factor of production?

options.label: A
options.text: Labour

options.label: B
options.text: Capital

options.label: C
options.text: Land

options.label: D
options.text: Enterprise

explanation: Land includes natural resources below the earth's surface, including mineral and oil deposits. It is not capital because it is not man-made.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A new apprenticeship improves workers' technical skills. What type of capital is primarily increased?

options.label: A
options.text: Human capital

options.label: B
options.text: Financial capital only

options.label: C
options.text: Natural capital only

options.label: D
options.text: Physical capital

explanation: An apprenticeship increases workers' knowledge and skills. These productive attributes are human capital rather than physical capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A manufacturer assigns one worker to cut material, another to sew it and another to attach buttons. What is this an example of?

options.label: A
options.text: A reduction in specialisation

options.label: B
options.text: Division of labour

options.label: C
options.text: Self-sufficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Enterprise

explanation: The production process has been split into separate stages, with each worker performing one task. This is the division of labour and results in greater task specialisation.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement about specialisation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater productivity can accompany greater dependence on exchange.

options.label: B
options.text: Greater productivity removes exposure to changing consumer demand.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater specialisation makes every producer independently self-sufficient.

options.label: D
options.text: Greater specialisation removes exposure to changing production technology.

explanation: Specialisation can increase output because producers concentrate on activities in which they have an advantage. However, specialists are not self-sufficient, so exchange becomes more important.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which action best represents the organising function of enterprise?

options.label: A
options.text: Receiving a wage for routine production work.

options.label: B
options.text: Purchasing products for the owner’s household consumption rather than combining productive resources to supply a marketable service.

options.label: C
options.text: Coordinating resources to produce a marketable service.

options.label: D
options.text: Supplying a natural mineral resource for extraction.

explanation: The organising role of enterprise involves bringing together land, labour and capital so that goods or services can be produced.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which of the following is capital in the economic sense?

options.label: A
options.text: The rainfall on the farm

options.label: B
options.text: A tractor used on a farm

options.label: C
options.text: Money kept in a household wallet

options.label: D
options.text: The farmer's physical effort

explanation: Capital in production means man-made aids used to produce output. A tractor is physical capital. Cash itself is not a productive machine, labour is human effort and rainfall is a natural resource.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which row correctly matches the factor of production to its usual reward?

options.label: A
options.text: Land – wages; labour – rent

options.label: B
options.text: Capital – profit; enterprise – interest

options.label: C
options.text: Capital – rent; enterprise – wages

options.label: D
options.text: Land – rent; labour – wages

explanation: Land receives rent and labour receives wages or salaries. Capital receives interest and enterprise receives profit.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A worker repeats the same narrow task on an assembly line. Which outcome is most consistent with the division of labour?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater output alongside greater worker self-sufficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower output alongside less dependence between stages.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater output alongside lower job satisfaction.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower output alongside greater worker task proficiency.

explanation: Division of labour can raise output and productivity because workers specialise, but repetitive work can also create monotony, boredom and dissatisfaction.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which person is performing the entrepreneurial risk-bearing role most directly?

options.label: A
options.text: A lender entitled to agreed interest payments rather than the uncertain residual return from the firm’s operations.

options.label: B
options.text: An employee entitled to an agreed wage.

options.label: C
options.text: A landlord entitled to agreed rental payments.

options.label: D
options.text: An owner exposed to uncertain residual profits.

explanation: The entrepreneur bears uncertainty over the outcome of production. An owner who can lose invested funds if the business fails is directly bearing that risk.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes land from capital?

options.label: A
options.text: Land consists entirely of fixed manufactured assets, whereas capital consists of unlimited natural resources.

options.label: B
options.text: Land earns wages; capital earns rent.

options.label: C
options.text: Land is skill; capital is effort.

options.label: D
options.text: Land is natural; capital is produced.

explanation: The key distinction is origin: land consists of natural resources, whereas capital consists of man-made aids used to produce goods and services.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A country spends more on technical education and less on importing industrial machinery. Other things equal, what is the most likely change over time?

options.label: A
options.text: Faster human-capital growth and faster physical-capital growth.

options.label: B
options.text: Slower human-capital growth and slower physical-capital growth.

options.label: C
options.text: Faster human-capital growth and slower physical-capital growth.

options.label: D
options.text: Slower human-capital growth and faster physical-capital growth.

explanation: Technical education develops workers' skills and therefore human capital. Industrial machinery is physical capital, so reducing machinery imports would, other things equal, reduce the addition to physical capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A fishing company uses the sea, crew members, boats and an owner who decides how to combine them. Which row classifies these resources correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: Sea: land; crew: labour; boats: capital; owner-organiser: enterprise

options.label: B
options.text: Sea: labour; crew: capital; boats: enterprise; owner-organiser: land

options.label: C
options.text: Sea: capital; crew: labour; boats: land; owner-organiser: enterprise

options.label: D
options.text: Sea: land; crew: enterprise; boats: capital; owner-organiser: labour

explanation: The sea is a natural resource and therefore land; crew members supply labour; boats are man-made productive assets and therefore capital; the person organising the other resources performs enterprise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why can the division of labour lower the unit cost of production?

options.label: A
options.text: Specialists gain proficiency in completing individual tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Every worker learns and performs every production stage.

options.label: C
options.text: Specialists remove the need for any productive equipment.

options.label: D
options.text: Every worker becomes independent of all input suppliers.

explanation: When workers specialise in particular tasks, repetition and concentration on a narrow activity can raise productivity. If more output is produced in a given time, unit costs can fall.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm buys a new computer-controlled cutting machine and also trains workers to operate it. What happens to its capital?

options.label: A
options.text: Physical capital rises; human capital stays unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Physical capital rises; human capital also rises.

options.label: C
options.text: Physical capital stays unchanged; human capital stays unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Human capital rises; physical capital stays unchanged.

explanation: The machine is physical capital because it is a man-made aid to production. Training improves workers' knowledge and skills, so it also increases human capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A farmer owns fertile soil, uses a tractor, employs two workers and decides what crop to plant despite uncertainty about future prices. Which factor is represented by the decision-making and risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Enterprise

options.label: B
options.text: Physical capital

options.label: C
options.text: Land

options.label: D
options.text: Labour

explanation: Choosing how to organise resources while accepting uncertainty over future prices is the entrepreneurial role. The soil is land, the tractor is capital and the employees provide labour.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which change is most likely to reduce one disadvantage of a highly specialised workforce?

options.label: A
options.text: Narrowing each worker’s responsibilities further and increasing repetition while reducing access to training for alternative occupations.

options.label: B
options.text: Restricting workers’ movement between different occupations.

options.label: C
options.text: Reducing workers’ access to additional training.

options.label: D
options.text: Training workers to perform several different tasks.

explanation: Highly specialised workers can become bored or vulnerable if their narrow skills become obsolete. Multi-skilling increases flexibility and can reduce both monotony and the risk of occupational immobility.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A software firm has skilled programmers, office space, computers and a founder who coordinates projects and accepts uncertain profits. Which two factors of production are most directly represented by the programmers and computers?

options.label: A
options.text: Capital and land

options.label: B
options.text: Labour and capital

options.label: C
options.text: Enterprise and labour

options.label: D
options.text: Land and enterprise

explanation: Programmers provide human effort and are therefore labour. Computers are man-made aids to production and are therefore capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A country's workers become highly specialised in producing a product whose demand later falls sharply. What is the most likely consequence?

options.label: A
options.text: Specialists become independent of all exchange with others.

options.label: B
options.text: Specialists automatically acquire the skills needed in unrelated industries as demand for their original product falls.

options.label: C
options.text: Unemployment rises when skills transfer poorly to other jobs.

options.label: D
options.text: Specialists become self-sufficient as their product demand declines.

explanation: Specialisation can make workers vulnerable when technology or demand changes. If specialist skills are not easily transferable to other activities, unemployment can result.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which is the best example of human capital rather than labour itself?

options.label: A
options.text: An engineer’s hours spent performing productive tasks during the current week rather than the qualifications acquired through training.

options.label: B
options.text: An engineer’s knowledge acquired through technical training.

options.label: C
options.text: A factory’s building used for engineering work.

options.label: D
options.text: A factory’s natural gas used during production.

explanation: Labour is the human effort supplied in production, whereas human capital is the stock of knowledge, skills and abilities embodied in the worker. Training increases that stock.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A business owner chooses a risky new product, hires workers and rents machinery. If the product succeeds, which factor reward is associated with the owner's entrepreneurial role?

options.label: A
options.text: Profit

options.label: B
options.text: Rent

options.label: C
options.text: Interest

options.label: D
options.text: Wages

explanation: The owner is performing enterprise by organising resources and bearing risk. Profit is the factor reward to enterprise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which combination is most likely to result from greater division of labour in a factory?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher productivity and greater task specialisation.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher job satisfaction and less task specialisation.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower productivity and greater worker self-sufficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: Greater worker self-sufficiency and less interdependence.

explanation: Division of labour allocates workers to narrower tasks, increasing task specialisation. Repetition and concentration on those tasks can raise productivity, although job satisfaction may fall.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A business uses a rented warehouse, hired workers and machines bought with borrowed funds. Which payment is the factor reward to the owner of the warehouse?

options.label: A
options.text: Rent

options.label: B
options.text: Wages

options.label: C
options.text: Interest

options.label: D
options.text: Profit

explanation: The warehouse site and premises are associated with the use of land/property, and the payment to its owner is rent. The workers receive wages, lenders may receive interest and enterprise receives profit.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An economy has many educated workers but very few machines and transport facilities. Which description is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Strong human capital and strong physical capital.

options.label: B
options.text: Weak human capital and weak physical capital.

options.label: C
options.text: Weak human capital and strong physical capital.

options.label: D
options.text: Strong human capital and weak physical capital.

explanation: Education and skills contribute to human capital. Machines and transport infrastructure are physical capital, so the economy can have strong human capital while lacking physical capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why does specialisation normally increase the need for trade?

options.label: A
options.text: Specialists need no goods outside their own output.

options.label: B
options.text: Specialists can independently produce the full range of goods they need, so they become self-sufficient as their tasks narrow.

options.label: C
options.text: Specialists produce a narrower range of goods than they consume.

options.label: D
options.text: Specialists cannot produce any surplus for exchange.

explanation: A specialist concentrates production in a narrower range of activities and is therefore not self-sufficient. Surplus output can be exchanged for the goods and services produced by other specialists.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which change most clearly increases the quantity of land as a usable factor of production?

options.label: A
options.text: Improving existing workers’ productive skills.

options.label: B
options.text: Installing additional manufactured production machinery.

options.label: C
options.text: Appointing additional managers to coordinate production.

options.label: D
options.text: Bringing previously unusable natural resources into production.

explanation: Land is the natural resource input. Making previously unusable natural land available for production increases the usable quantity of land; the other changes affect labour, capital or enterprise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A highly specialised factory has very high output, but absenteeism rises because workers dislike repetitive jobs. What does this show?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher output per worker establishes that employees prefer increasingly repetitive tasks and therefore cannot suffer boredom.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher productivity prevents boredom from repetitive production work.

options.label: C
options.text: Productivity gains can accompany dissatisfaction with repetitive work.

options.label: D
options.text: Greater specialisation removes the need to assess employee responses.

explanation: The case combines two recognised effects of division of labour: task specialisation can raise output, while monotonous repetitive work can reduce job satisfaction and increase dissatisfaction.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which statement about entrepreneurs in large modern companies is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Every shareholder manages every daily production decision.

options.label: B
options.text: Managers may organise production while owners bear risk.

options.label: C
options.text: Large firms dispense with any entrepreneurial organising function.

options.label: D
options.text: Only employees receiving fixed salaries bear business risk.

explanation: The entrepreneurial functions remain important in large firms, but they can be divided. Salaried managers may organise resources while owners or shareholders bear much of the financial risk.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A factory replaces some routine manual work with automated machinery but retrains the remaining employees for technical roles. Which pair of changes is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Less machinery and greater skill among retrained workers.

options.label: B
options.text: More machinery and lower skill among retrained workers.

options.label: C
options.text: More machinery and greater skill among retrained workers.

options.label: D
options.text: Less machinery and lower skill among retrained workers.

explanation: Automation adds machinery and therefore physical capital. Retraining improves the skills of workers who remain, so their human capital also rises.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which factor of production is correctly paired with an example?

options.label: A
options.text: Capital: an employee’s work during a shift.

options.label: B
options.text: Enterprise: coordinating workers and machinery in production.

options.label: C
options.text: Labour: an underground mineral deposit awaiting extraction.

options.label: D
options.text: Land: manufactured equipment installed during the year to process naturally occurring raw materials into finished products.

explanation: Enterprise is the organising and risk-bearing input. A machine is capital, worker effort is labour and a mineral deposit is land.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A region specialises heavily in one export industry. Which event creates the greatest risk from this specialisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Specialists improve their existing product’s quality.

options.label: B
options.text: World demand for the specialist product permanently declines.

options.label: C
options.text: Specialists become more proficient at production tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: Producers gain reliable access to exchange with outsiders.

explanation: Regional specialisation can raise efficiency, but dependence on a narrow range of products creates vulnerability. A lasting fall in demand can reduce output and employment in the specialised region.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which payment is not a reward to a factor of production?

options.label: A
options.text: Rent received for productive land.

options.label: B
options.text: Interest received by a lender for supplying funds used to purchase productive capital equipment.

options.label: C
options.text: Benefits received without productive-factor provision.

options.label: D
options.text: Wages received for productive labour.

explanation: Factor rewards are payments for supplying productive resources: rent, wages, interest and profit. A transfer payment is made without a current productive contribution and is therefore not a factor reward.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A firm can increase output because each worker concentrates on one stage and becomes very proficient at it. Which chain best explains the change?

options.label: A
options.text: Division of labour → less specialisation → lower productivity

options.label: B
options.text: Division of labour → task specialisation → higher productivity

options.label: C
options.text: Specialisation → every worker completes the whole product → higher output

options.label: D
options.text: Self-sufficiency → less exchange → higher productivity

explanation: Division of labour breaks production into tasks. Workers then specialise in particular tasks, and repeated performance can increase proficiency and productivity, raising output.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A new restaurant owner leases premises, hires chefs and buys kitchen equipment. Which activity specifically demonstrates enterprise rather than the supply of another factor?

options.label: A
options.text: Providing the site used for production.

options.label: B
options.text: Providing chefs’ time spent preparing meals.

options.label: C
options.text: Coordinating premises, workers and cooking equipment.

options.label: D
options.text: Supplying the manufactured kitchen equipment used by the chefs rather than deciding how to combine productive resources.

explanation: Enterprise is the coordinating function that combines land, labour and capital. The other options describe the use of labour, capital and land themselves.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which comparison between physical and human capital is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Physical capital: naturally occurring resources used in production; human capital: manufactured equipment operated by employees.

options.label: B
options.text: Physical: wage payments; human: rental payments.

options.label: C
options.text: Physical: unproductive assets; human: guaranteed productivity.

options.label: D
options.text: Physical: productive assets; human: acquired capabilities.

explanation: Physical capital consists of man-made productive assets such as machinery, while human capital consists of productive knowledge and skills embodied in people.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A firm divides production into many narrow tasks. Which outcome would most weaken the case for increasing the division of labour further?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher output per worker through task proficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Severe boredom raising absenteeism and production errors.

options.label: C
options.text: Better matching of employees to suitable tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: Employees gain further experience in their assigned tasks, helping them perform each task more accurately and quickly.

explanation: Division of labour can raise productivity, but if tasks become excessively repetitive, boredom and dissatisfaction can reduce attendance or quality. This can offset some of the efficiency gain.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A country encourages workers to learn several occupations rather than one very narrow skill. Which disadvantage of specialisation is this policy most directly intended to reduce?

options.label: A
options.text: The possibility that tasks become more productive.

options.label: B
options.text: The possibility that workers gain task proficiency.

options.label: C
options.text: The need for exchange between specialist producers.

options.label: D
options.text: The risk that narrow skills become obsolete.

explanation: Multi-skilling improves occupational flexibility. It reduces the danger that workers with a single specialist skill become unemployed when technology or consumer demand changes.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement best explains why profit is associated with enterprise rather than labour?

options.label: A
options.text: Profit is fixed remuneration for hours worked.

options.label: B
options.text: Profit is agreed remuneration for land supplied.

options.label: C
options.text: Profit is guaranteed remuneration for funds lent.

options.label: D
options.text: Profit is residual remuneration for entrepreneurial activity.

explanation: Labour is usually paid wages or salaries for work performed. Profit is the residual and uncertain return to enterprise for organising resources and bearing the risk of production.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A business has four resources: a mineral deposit, geologists, drilling equipment and a founder who raises funds and coordinates production. Which sequence identifies the four factors?

options.label: A
options.text: Land, labour, capital, enterprise

options.label: B
options.text: Land, enterprise, capital, labour

options.label: C
options.text: Labour, land, enterprise, capital

options.label: D
options.text: Capital, labour, land, enterprise

explanation: The mineral deposit is land, geologists provide labour, drilling equipment is capital and the founder performs enterprise by coordinating resources and bearing risk.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why may national specialisation raise living standards?

options.label: A
options.text: Specialisation prevents changes in consumers’ product preferences.

options.label: B
options.text: Specialisation removes the need to import other products.

options.label: C
options.text: Specialisation requires every worker to make every product.

options.label: D
options.text: Productive advantages and exchange expand consumption opportunities.

explanation: National specialisation can increase the output obtained from available resources. Surplus output can then be traded for other goods and services, allowing consumption possibilities and living standards to rise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which change is most likely to increase both the quality of labour and the productivity of existing physical capital?

options.label: A
options.text: Leaving productive machinery unused for longer periods.

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing workers’ training in existing production methods.

options.label: C
options.text: Replacing trained operators with workers lacking technical skills.

options.label: D
options.text: Training workers to use existing machinery effectively.

explanation: Training raises human capital. Better-skilled workers can use existing machines more effectively, so the productive contribution of the physical capital can also increase even though its quantity is unchanged.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm's owner delegates daily management to salaried professionals but keeps ownership of the business. Which entrepreneurial function does the owner most clearly continue to bear?

options.label: A
options.text: Supplying the business’s natural resources.

options.label: B
options.text: Performing all daily managerial tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Performing all routine production work.

options.label: D
options.text: Bearing the business’s financial risk.

explanation: Delegating management can separate the organising role from ownership. The owner still bears the risk that the value of the business and its profits may fall.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement about the quantity and quality of factors of production is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Large labour quantities can coexist with low skill levels.

options.label: B
options.text: Additional machinery removes every requirement for entrepreneurial organisation.

options.label: C
options.text: Large labour quantities establish equally high worker skill levels.

options.label: D
options.text: Additional land establishes identical productivity for every natural resource.

explanation: The quantity of labour and the quality of labour are different. A country may have many workers but relatively low levels of education, training or skills, so human capital can still be limited.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A car factory changes from each worker building an entire car to each worker performing one repeated stage. Which result is most likely in the short term?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater task specialisation may raise worker productivity.

options.label: B
options.text: Less task specialisation necessarily reduces worker productivity.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater task specialisation makes every input internally available.

options.label: D
options.text: Less task specialisation removes the need to organise production.

explanation: Breaking the process into stages is division of labour. Workers specialise in particular tasks, which can raise productivity and output per worker.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which situation most clearly shows entrepreneurial organisation without the entrepreneur personally supplying the other factors?

options.label: A
options.text: A landlord receives rent for a productive site.

options.label: B
options.text: A lender receives interest for providing borrowed funds.

options.label: C
options.text: A founder coordinates resources rented from other owners.

options.label: D
options.text: An employee receives wages for routine production work.

explanation: The founder coordinates resources supplied by others. Enterprise does not require the entrepreneur to own the land, perform all labour or own all physical capital; the key function is organising them and bearing risk.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which row correctly identifies the effect of two changes on human and physical capital?

options.label: A
options.text: More worker training: neither human nor physical capital changes; more machinery: neither human nor physical capital changes

options.label: B
options.text: More worker training: human capital rises; more machinery: physical capital rises

options.label: C
options.text: More worker training: physical capital rises; more machinery: human capital rises

options.label: D
options.text: More worker training: human capital falls; more machinery: physical capital falls

explanation: Training develops skills embodied in people and therefore human capital. Machinery is a man-made productive asset and therefore physical capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A specialised worker loses a job after a new technology makes the worker's narrow skill unnecessary. Which statement is best supported?

options.label: A
options.text: Narrow skills guarantee that specialist workers can immediately move into any other occupation without further training.

options.label: B
options.text: Narrow skills can raise productivity but increase vulnerability.

options.label: C
options.text: New technology cannot affect demand for specialist workers.

options.label: D
options.text: Narrow skills remove workers’ need for additional training.

explanation: The case illustrates a trade-off. Specialisation can raise productivity while the skill remains valuable, but a narrow skill can become obsolete when technology changes, creating a need for retraining.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which is the clearest difference between an entrepreneur and a salaried worker?

options.label: A
options.text: Entrepreneur: uncertain residual return; employee: agreed wage.

options.label: B
options.text: Entrepreneurs receive a fixed agreed wage; salaried employees receive the uncertain return left after all other business payments.

options.label: C
options.text: Entrepreneur: rental income; employee: interest income.

options.label: D
options.text: Entrepreneur: interest income; employee: rental income.

explanation: A salaried worker supplies labour in return for an agreed wage or salary. Enterprise is distinguished by the functions of organising production and bearing business risk, with profit as the reward.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why may division of labour improve the quality of a finished product?

options.label: A
options.text: Repetition improves proficiency at particular production stages.

options.label: B
options.text: One worker without relevant training carries out all production stages, replacing workers who specialise in particular tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Workers constantly switch between unfamiliar production tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: Specialisation prevents the acquisition of relevant experience.

explanation: Workers who repeatedly perform a particular task can become more proficient at it. Greater proficiency can reduce mistakes and improve the quality of the finished product.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country has a rapidly growing working-age population but weak schooling and little vocational training. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: Population growth establishes equally rapid worker skill growth.

options.label: B
options.text: Labour quantity may grow faster than skill quality.

options.label: C
options.text: Population growth establishes equally rapid machinery-stock growth.

options.label: D
options.text: Labour quantity and worker skill become identical measures.

explanation: A larger working-age population can increase the quantity of labour available. Human capital depends on skills, knowledge and training, so weak education means the quality of labour may not improve at the same rate.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A manufacturer is considering further division of labour. Output per worker would probably rise, but employee turnover is already high because jobs are repetitive. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Worker dissatisfaction makes all productivity gains irrelevant.

options.label: B
options.text: Worker turnover establishes insufficient specialisation of tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Assess productivity gains against dissatisfaction and turnover costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Higher output per worker justifies further division of labour regardless of any extra costs from turnover and employee dissatisfaction.

explanation: Division of labour can improve productivity, but excessive repetition can reduce job satisfaction and raise turnover or absenteeism. The overall effect depends on the relative size of these gains and costs.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A mining company uses a natural ore deposit, autonomous trucks, trained technicians and shareholders who may lose their investment. Which pair represents land and enterprise respectively?

options.label: A
options.text: The ore deposit and risk-bearing shareholders.

options.label: B
options.text: The risk-bearing shareholders and trained technicians.

options.label: C
options.text: The trained technicians and autonomous trucks.

options.label: D
options.text: The autonomous trucks and ore deposit.

explanation: The ore deposit is a natural resource and therefore land. In a large company, shareholders may bear the financial risk associated with enterprise, while managers may carry out much of the organising function.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government funds retraining for workers displaced from a highly specialised industry. Which two effects are most directly intended?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower skills and greater repetition of narrow tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher skills and greater adaptability to occupational change.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater self-sufficiency and less exchange between different producers.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower adaptability and greater dependence on obsolete skills.

explanation: Retraining builds new skills and therefore human capital. It also addresses a key disadvantage of specialisation: workers can become unemployed when their narrow specialist skills are no longer demanded.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A founder contributes no land and no machinery personally, but designs the business model, hires the resources and accepts the possibility of losing the initial investment. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Business decisions constitute labour without any entrepreneurial role.

options.label: B
options.text: Enterprise requires ownership of every natural resource used.

options.label: C
options.text: Enterprise does not require ownership of other factors.

options.label: D
options.text: Enterprise requires ownership of every machine used in production.

explanation: Enterprise is defined by organising the other factors and bearing risk, not by personally owning the land or capital. The founder can therefore supply enterprise while hiring or renting other factors.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm's new machinery doubles potential output, but workers are not trained to use it effectively. What does this show about physical and human capital?

options.label: A
options.text: Additional training reduces the productivity of installed machinery.

options.label: B
options.text: Additional machinery removes every need for worker training.

options.label: C
options.text: Weak complementary skills can limit machinery’s productivity benefits.

options.label: D
options.text: Worker skills have no effect on machinery’s productive use.

explanation: Physical and human capital can complement each other. Additional machinery raises physical capital, but the output gain may be limited if workers lack the knowledge and skills needed to operate it effectively.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A specialised region produces only one major export. Productivity is high, but a substitute product is developed abroad. Which outcome best captures the economic trade-off?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher productivity prevents any decline in product demand.

options.label: B
options.text: Greater specialisation immediately improves transferability of workers’ skills.

options.label: C
options.text: Productivity gains can accompany vulnerability to falling demand.

options.label: D
options.text: Foreign substitutes increase the specialist region’s productive self-sufficiency.

explanation: Specialisation can generate high productivity while demand is strong. However, dependence on a narrow output makes the region vulnerable to changes in technology or preferences, which can reduce demand and employment.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which observation most strongly suggests that a firm's entrepreneurial functions are separated?

options.label: A
options.text: The company pays contractual rent for its premises and agreed interest on its loans while the owner also manages daily operations.

options.label: B
options.text: Managers organise production while shareholders bear financial risk.

options.label: C
options.text: The firm combines natural resources with employees’ work.

options.label: D
options.text: Workers receive wages while using the firm’s machinery.

explanation: Separation of entrepreneurial functions occurs when organisation and risk-bearing are performed by different groups. Managers may organise the other factors while shareholders bear the financial consequences of failure.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm's output rises after workers are assigned narrower tasks. Which evidence would most weaken the claim that the output rise was caused by division of labour?

options.label: A
options.text: Production was divided into more specialist stages.

options.label: B
options.text: Workers spend more time repeating their assigned tasks and become more experienced at the specialist stages they perform.

options.label: C
options.text: Workers performed fewer stages of the production process.

options.label: D
options.text: Faster machinery was installed alongside the task changes.

explanation: If physical capital also improved, the higher output cannot confidently be attributed to division of labour alone. The machinery provides an alternative explanation for the productivity increase.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A company pays wages to staff, rent for a site, interest on borrowed funds and a residual return to its owner. If sales revenue unexpectedly falls, which payment is most directly associated with the risk-bearing factor?

options.label: A
options.text: The owner's residual profit

options.label: B
options.text: The agreed wage payment

options.label: C
options.text: The contracted rent payment

options.label: D
options.text: The contracted interest payment

explanation: Profit is the uncertain residual reward to enterprise. Wages, rent and interest are payments to other factors and may be contractually due even when the entrepreneur's profit falls.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country increases university education but cuts spending on factory equipment by the same amount. Which conclusion can be made without additional information?

options.label: A
options.text: Education spending increases the stock of productive machinery.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced equipment spending necessarily lowers workers’ skill levels.

options.label: C
options.text: Human capital rises; the net capacity effect is uncertain.

options.label: D
options.text: Equal spending changes necessarily leave productive capacity unchanged.

explanation: Education tends to raise human capital, while reduced equipment spending may slow the growth of physical capital. Without information about their relative productivity effects, the net effect on productive capacity cannot be determined.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A firm considering extreme task specialisation expects a 12% rise in output but also expects product defects to rise because bored workers pay less attention. What is the best economic judgement?

options.label: A
options.text: Compare employee satisfaction while disregarding output and quality.

options.label: B
options.text: Compare additional output while disregarding quality and dissatisfaction costs.

options.label: C
options.text: Reject every specialisation scheme whenever any product defects occur.

options.label: D
options.text: Compare extra output’s value with additional quality and dissatisfaction costs.

explanation: The gain from greater division of labour is not measured by output alone. A sound judgement compares the productivity benefit with costs such as defects, absenteeism, turnover and worker dissatisfaction.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A worker's experience improves, a firm buys another machine, and a new mineral deposit is discovered. Which sequence of factor changes is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: More machinery, more natural resources, greater entrepreneurship.

options.label: B
options.text: More natural resources, greater work effort, more machinery.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater entrepreneurship, more machinery, greater work effort.

options.label: D
options.text: Greater skills, more machinery, more natural resources.

explanation: Experience improves the productive quality of labour through human capital. A machine adds physical capital. A mineral deposit is a natural resource and therefore adds land.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A worker leaves a narrowly specialised occupation because demand has collapsed and cannot quickly move to another job. Which feature of specialisation is most relevant?

options.label: A
options.text: Narrow skills make workers equally suited to every occupation.

options.label: B
options.text: Narrow skills remove the need to acquire new capabilities.

options.label: C
options.text: Narrow skills increase mobility when the specialised market contracts.

options.label: D
options.text: Narrow skills can limit mobility when demand changes.

explanation: A narrow specialist skill may be highly productive in one occupation but not easily transferable. When demand changes, this can create unemployment unless the worker retrains or becomes multi-skilled.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A manager is paid a fixed salary to coordinate production but owns no shares. Shareholders receive any profit and may suffer a capital loss. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Managers organise production; shareholders bear business risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Managers organise production; shareholders supply routine work.

options.label: C
options.text: Managers bear all losses; shareholders organise daily production.

options.label: D
options.text: Managers supply natural resources; shareholders supply routine work.

explanation: Contemporary large firms may separate the two entrepreneurial functions. Managers can organise production while shareholders bear financial risk through uncertain profits and changes in the value of their ownership.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm increases division of labour and then finds that one absent specialist stops an entire stage of production. Which disadvantage does this most directly reveal?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete independence of each specialised production worker.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced specialisation across the different production stages.

options.label: C
options.text: Greater flexibility across every specialised production task.

options.label: D
options.text: Greater interdependence among specialised production stages.

explanation: When each worker or team performs a narrow stage, the stages become interdependent. Disruption to one specialist task can therefore affect the wider production process.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which policy would most directly improve human capital without directly increasing the stock of physical capital?

options.label: A
options.text: Subsidising new factory-building construction.

options.label: B
options.text: Subsidising new production machinery.

options.label: C
options.text: Subsidising additional industrial robots.

options.label: D
options.text: Subsidising workers’ vocational retraining.

explanation: Vocational retraining develops skills embodied in people and therefore human capital. Robots, buildings and machinery are physical capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: An entrepreneur chooses between a safe project with a small expected profit and a risky project with a larger possible profit but a chance of loss. Which aspect of enterprise is central to this decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Bearing uncertainty over business outcomes.

options.label: B
options.text: Eliminating every productive opportunity cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Providing natural resources for extraction.

options.label: D
options.text: Receiving guaranteed remuneration for work.

explanation: The entrepreneur must decide whether the possible higher return justifies the greater risk. This uncertainty over profit or loss is a defining feature of enterprise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which situation would most likely reduce the benefit from national specialisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Specialist producers become more proficient in their tasks while foreign buyers continue to demand the products they export.

options.label: B
options.text: Trade disruption prevents imports of other required goods.

options.label: C
options.text: Surplus production can be exchanged more reliably.

options.label: D
options.text: Workers gain proficiency in their specialist tasks.

explanation: Specialisation reduces self-sufficiency and increases dependence on exchange. If trade is disrupted, the country may struggle to obtain products it has stopped producing itself.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A firm says its capital has increased because it has accumulated more cash in a bank account, although it has bought no new productive assets. Why might an economist disagree?

options.label: A
options.text: Money is labour because transactions require effort.

options.label: B
options.text: Money is land because it represents natural resources.

options.label: C
options.text: Productive capital is machinery and assets, not cash.

options.label: D
options.text: Money is enterprise because bank deposits earn interest.

explanation: In factor-of-production analysis, capital refers to productive man-made assets such as tools, machinery and buildings. Money can finance those assets but is not itself necessarily a physical aid to production.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country has highly specialised workers in an industry that is expanding rapidly today but faces a high probability of automation in five years. Which policy would best preserve the current productivity benefit while reducing future risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Narrow tasks further and prohibit retraining.

options.label: B
options.text: End productive specialisation without developing replacement skills.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep specialisation while developing transferable skills.

options.label: D
options.text: Prevent specialists acquiring skills outside their current tasks.

explanation: The country can retain the present productivity gains from specialisation while improving workers' ability to adapt later. Transferable skills and multi-skilling reduce vulnerability if technology makes the current specialist skills redundant.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A firm's founder identifies a market opportunity, arranges finance, hires workers and rents equipment. Which statement best explains why these actions are classified as enterprise rather than capital?

options.label: A
options.text: They provide the firm’s manufactured production equipment.

options.label: B
options.text: They coordinate resources and involve entrepreneurial risk-taking.

options.label: C
options.text: They supply the firm’s natural productive resources.

options.label: D
options.text: They provide routine work for guaranteed hourly wages.

explanation: Capital is the stock of man-made productive assets. Enterprise is the decision-making function that organises land, labour and capital and accepts the uncertainty of the business outcome.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A factory's workers are highly productive after years of task specialisation. A new product design requires workers to perform several unfamiliar tasks. What is the main risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Past success in narrow tasks guarantees that the workforce can perform all unfamiliar tasks required by the new design.

options.label: B
options.text: Past productivity eliminates the need for additional training.

options.label: C
options.text: Changed production requirements may make narrow skills less useful.

options.label: D
options.text: Narrow skills ensure flexibility across every new production task.

explanation: Specialisation builds proficiency in a narrow task, but that proficiency may not transfer when products or technologies change. The firm may need retraining or multi-skilling.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A business loses money even though its managers have organised production efficiently. Which conclusion about enterprise is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Efficient organisation guarantees a positive residual return.

options.label: B
options.text: Financial losses establish that no enterprise was supplied.

options.label: C
options.text: Market uncertainty arises only from inefficient production organisation.

options.label: D
options.text: Efficient organisation does not eliminate business uncertainty.

explanation: Enterprise involves both organisation and risk. Even well-organised production can make a loss if demand, prices or other conditions turn out unfavourably.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which combination of changes is most likely to increase both human capital and the benefits of specialisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Less training alongside random assignment to unfamiliar tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: More machinery alongside restrictions on relevant worker training.

options.label: C
options.text: Better training alongside tasks matching workers’ skills.

options.label: D
options.text: Less skill development alongside lower task proficiency.

explanation: Training increases human capital. Assigning workers to tasks in which those skills are useful allows specialisation to convert the improved skills into higher productivity and quality.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A firm is deciding whether to replace a broad craft job with ten separate specialist jobs. Which information is least sufficient on its own to justify the change?

options.label: A
options.text: The expected change in motivation and errors.

options.label: B
options.text: The expected change in finished product quality.

options.label: C
options.text: The available number of separate production tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: The expected change in output per worker.

explanation: Knowing that a process can be divided does not show whether doing so is worthwhile. The decision requires evidence about benefits such as productivity and quality and costs such as boredom, errors or turnover.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A worker receives a salary, a landlord receives rent, a bank receives interest and an owner receives uncertain profit. Which payment would be most likely to fall to zero or become negative if the business performs very badly?

options.label: A
options.text: The bank's contracted interest

options.label: B
options.text: The owner's profit

options.label: C
options.text: The worker's contracted salary

options.label: D
options.text: The landlord's contracted rent

explanation: Profit is the residual reward to enterprise and is directly exposed to business performance. The other payments are factor rewards that may be contractually due even when the firm makes little or no profit.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.3 rewards to the factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country has abundant natural resources and labour but weak infrastructure and little entrepreneurial experience. Which pair of factors is relatively scarce?

options.label: A
options.text: Capital and enterprise

options.label: B
options.text: Land and labour

options.label: C
options.text: Labour and enterprise

options.label: D
options.text: Land and capital

explanation: Infrastructure is physical capital, while entrepreneurial experience contributes to enterprise. The country is stated to have abundant natural resources and labour, so land and labour are not the relatively scarce factors.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.1 nature and definition of factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A large corporation's board, acting on behalf of its owners, approves a risky expansion. Executives organise the new factories and employees carry out production. Which group performs the entrepreneurial role collectively?

options.label: A
options.text: Customers, whose purchases determine demand for the output and who therefore organise the corporation’s production resources.

options.label: B
options.text: The board and executives, deciding on risks and organising production.

options.label: C
options.text: Landowners, whose sites accommodate the new factory buildings.

options.label: D
options.text: Employees, whose routine work carries out production tasks.

explanation: In a complex modern firm, the entrepreneurial functions need not be performed by one person. Decision-makers who accept strategic risk and managers who organise the factors can together perform enterprise.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.5 role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: risk and organisation of the other factors of production | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which condition would make the productivity advantage of division of labour least likely to persist?

options.label: A
options.text: Severe monotony raises errors and labour turnover.

options.label: B
options.text: Workers are matched to tasks they perform well.

options.label: C
options.text: Repetition increases workers’ proficiency at assigned tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: Production stages are coordinated without unnecessary delays.

explanation: The productivity gain from task specialisation can be undermined if boredom causes mistakes, absenteeism or turnover. The other conditions support rather than weaken the productivity advantage.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government can spend the same amount either on training nurses or buying hospital scanners. Which statement is correct about the type of capital created?

options.label: A
options.text: Training: human capital; scanners: physical capital.

options.label: B
options.text: Nurse training creates physical capital; hospital scanners also create physical capital, rather than human capital.

options.label: C
options.text: Training: human capital; scanners: human capital.

options.label: D
options.text: Training: physical capital; scanners: human capital.

explanation: Training raises knowledge and skills embodied in workers and therefore human capital. Scanners are man-made productive assets and therefore physical capital.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.2 difference between human capital and physical capital | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A specialist producer can make twice as much output after concentrating on one product, but now depends entirely on others for food and transport. Which conclusion is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher productivity alongside less need for exchange.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher productivity alongside greater dependence on exchange.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower productivity alongside greater dependence on exchange.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower productivity alongside greater productive self-sufficiency.

explanation: The producer's higher output shows the productive benefit of specialisation. However, concentrating on one product means relying on exchange to obtain other goods and services, so interdependence rises.
reference: 1.3 Factors of production | 1.3.4 division of labour and specialisation | AO2 Analysis
